```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
```

# Problem 1
```{r load-noaa}
data("ny_noaa")

ny_noaa
glimpse(ny_noaa)
```

```{r noaa-summary}
nrow(ny_noaa)
ncol(ny_noaa)
n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)

ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    prcp = round(mean(is.na(prcp)) * 100, 1),
    snow = round(mean(is.na(snow)) * 100, 1),
    snwd = round(mean(is.na(snwd)) * 100, 1),
    tmax = round(mean(is.na(tmax)) * 100, 1),
    tmin = round(mean(is.na(tmin)) * 100, 1)
  )
```
The NY NOAA dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables from 747 weather stations. Each row represents a daily weather record from one station. The variables include station ID, date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, and maximum and minimum temperatures. Missing data are relatively common, especially for maximum and minimum temperatures, which both have 43.7% missing values. Snow depth has 22.8% missing values, followed by 14.7% of snowfall and 5.6% of precipitation.

```{r clean-noaa}
ny_noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(date),
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )

glimpse(ny_noaa_clean)
```

```{r snowfall-summary}
ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  head(10)
```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm, with 2,008,508 observations, since most days have no snowfall. Other common values include 25 mm, 13 mm, 51 mm, and 76 mm. These values are approximately equivalent to 1, 0.5, 2, and 3 inches, which may be related to how snowfall was originally measured and converted into millimeters.


```{r average-temperature}
temp_data =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(is.finite(mean_tmax))

temp_data
```

```{r temperature-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
temp_data |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The average maximum temperature in July is much higher than that in January. January temperatures show greater variation across stations and years, while July temperatures are mostly between 20°C and 33°C. There is no clear increasing or decreasing trend over time. A few possible outliers can be observed, including an unusually low temperature of around 14°C in July and some January temperatures below -10°C.

```{r tmax-tmin-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
tmax_tmin_plot =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax), !is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 50) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The plot shows a positive relationship between minimum and maximum temperatures. As minimum temperature increases, maximum temperature also tends to increase. Most observations are concentrated along a diagonal pattern, while a few values fall far from the main distribution and may be outliers.


```{r snowfall-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
snowfall_plot =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = snow, group = year)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The distribution of snowfall is relatively similar across years, with a median of around 25 mm in most years. The middle 50% of snowfall values generally falls between approximately 13 mm and 51 mm. A few years have higher snowfall outliers, but there is no clear long-term trend in the distribution.

```{r combined-plot, fig.width=14, fig.height=6}
tmax_tmin_plot + snowfall_plot
```
The first plot shows a positive relationship between minimum and maximum temperatures, with most observations concentrated along a diagonal pattern. A few observations fall far from the main distribution and may be outliers. The second plot shows that the distribution of snowfall is relatively similar across years. The median snowfall is around 25 mm in most years, and the middle 50% of values generally falls between 13 mm and 51 mm. Some years have higher snowfall outliers, but there is no clear long-term trend.

# Problem 2
```{r load-nhanes}
nhanes_covar =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4)

nhanes_accel =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")

glimpse(nhanes_covar)
dim(nhanes_accel)

nhanes_accel |>
  select(SEQN, min1:min5) |>
  head()
```

```{r clean-nhanes-covar}
nhanes_covar_clean =
  nhanes_covar |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

head(nhanes_covar_clean)
```

```{r tidy-nhanes-accel}
nhanes_accel_long =
  nhanes_accel |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(minute)
  )

head(nhanes_accel_long)
```

```{r merge-nhanes}
nhanes_df =
  inner_join(
    nhanes_covar_clean,
    nhanes_accel_long,
    by = "SEQN"
  )

nhanes_df |>
  summarize(
    participants = n_distinct(SEQN),
    observations = n()
  )

head(nhanes_df)
```

```{r sex-education-table}
nhanes_covar_clean |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Number of Participants by Sex and Education"
  )
```
There are 118 men and 110 women in the cleaned dataset. Most participants have more than a high school education, with 56 men and 59 women in this category. The number of men and women is relatively similar in the other categories, except for the high school equivalent group, which has more men.

```{r age-distribution, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
nhanes_covar_clean |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (Years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
The age distributions differ across education levels. Participants with more than a high school education tend to be younger, with median ages around 40–45 years. In the high school equivalent group, women have a higher median age than men, while the age distributions are relatively similar for men and women with less than a high school education.

```{r total-activity}
nhanes_total =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(SEQN, sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

head(nhanes_total)
```

```{r total-activity-plot, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
nhanes_total |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Total daily activity tends to decrease with age across all three education groups. This decline is more noticeable among participants with less than a high school education, while those with more than a high school education show a relatively smaller decline. Women generally have higher fitted activity levels than men in the high school equivalent and more than high school groups. However, there is considerable variation in total activity among participants of similar ages.

```{r activity-by-minute}
nhanes_time =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hour = (minute - 1) / 60
  )

head(nhanes_time)
```

```{r activity-timecourse, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
nhanes_time |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.15, se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~education) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 4)) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns by Sex and Education",
    x = "Time of Day (Hours)",
    y = "Average MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The three education groups show similar daily activity patterns. Average activity is lowest during the early morning hours, increases rapidly after around 6 AM, and remains relatively high during the daytime before decreasing in the evening. Men and women have similar activity patterns in the less than high school group. In the other two education groups, women generally have higher average activity during the day, especially among participants with more than a high school education.

# Problem 3

```{r check-citibike-files}
list.files("data", recursive = TRUE)
```

```{r load-citibike}
citi_jan_2020 =
  read_csv("data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv")

citi_july_2020 =
  read_csv("data/July 2020 Citi.csv")

citi_jan_2024 =
  read_csv("data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv")

citi_july_2024 =
  read_csv("data/July 2024 Citi.csv")
```

```{r inspect-citibike}
glimpse(citi_jan_2020)
glimpse(citi_jan_2024)

nrow(citi_jan_2020)
nrow(citi_july_2020)
nrow(citi_jan_2024)
nrow(citi_july_2024)
```

```{r clean-citibike}
citi_df =
  bind_rows(
    citi_jan_2020 |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "January"),
    citi_july_2020 |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "July"),
    citi_jan_2024 |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "January"),
    citi_july_2024 |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type)
  )

glimpse(citi_df)
```

```{r check-citibike}
citi_df |>
  count(year, month)

citi_df |>
  count(member_casual)

citi_df |>
  count(rideable_type)

citi_df |>
  summarize(
    missing_duration = sum(is.na(duration)),
    missing_station = sum(is.na(start_station_name)),
    missing_membership = sum(is.na(member_casual))
  )
```
The Citi Bike dataset contains 99,485 rides from January and July of 2020 and 2024. I combined the four datasets and added year and month variables. The resulting dataset has 9 variables, including ride duration, bike type, starting and ending stations, day of the week, and membership status. There are 79,862 rides made by members and 19,623 by casual riders. There are 43 missing values for starting station names, while duration and membership status have no missing values.

```{r rides-membership-table}
citi_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  arrange(year, month) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Number of Rides by Year, Month, and Membership"
  )
```
Members had more rides than casual riders in all four months. The number of rides was higher in July than in January for both years, which may be related to warmer weather and more outdoor activities during summer. Ride counts were also higher in 2024 than in 2020 for both months. Casual riders accounted for a larger proportion of rides in July, while members made up most of the rides in January.

```{r top-stations}
citi_df |>
  filter(
    year == 2024,
    month == "July",
    !is.na(start_station_name)
  ) |>
  count(start_station_name) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  head(5) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Starting Station", "Number of Rides"),
    caption = "Top 5 Starting Stations in July 2024"
  )
```
In July 2024, Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers was the most popular starting station in the sample, with 163 rides, followed by University Pl & E 14 St with 155 rides. The five most popular stations had relatively similar ride counts, ranging from 146 to 163.

```{r median-duration}
citi_duration =
  citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

head(citi_duration)
```

```{r median-duration-plot, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
citi_duration |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = weekdays,
      y = median_duration,
      color = month,
      group = month
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Day of Week, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (Minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```
Median ride duration was higher in July than in January in both years. Rides also tended to be longer on weekends, especially in July 2020, when the median duration reached around 16.5 minutes on Saturday and Sunday. Compared with 2020, median ride duration was generally shorter in 2024 for both months. The difference between weekdays and weekends was also less noticeable in 2024.

```{r duration-distribution, fig.width=12, fig.height=6}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rideable_type, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_grid(member_casual ~ month) +
  scale_y_sqrt() +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration Distribution in 2024",
    x = "Bike Type",
    y = "Ride Duration (Minutes)",
    fill = "Bike Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
The plot shows that casual riders generally have longer ride duration than members, with a wider distribution of values. Among casual riders, classic bikes tend to have longer rides than electric bikes, while the difference is less noticeable among members. Ride durations also vary between January and July, although the distributions overlap considerably. Most rides are relatively short, with a smaller number of rides lasting much longer.
